February 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 3
Technology changes are coming our way! Upgrades
to communication tools; membership signup; and
website continuation/management are the driving
forces behind a team currently making this happen.
Firstly, don’t panic! Our standard of communication, as currently delivered by Brian Lunt, is not
affected. What is changing is a better back-end for
him and others to communicate club events. Secondly, the membership signup process will become
personalized and automated, thereby relieving our
secretary, treasurer, and communications officer of
a lot of tedious work. Lastly, the website will be migrated to a content resource management
platform. This will change the appearance of our
website however it will add new features for our
members.
In short, everything that we currently have or do
will remain but there will be more tools - better
tools - for all of us to engage in. The hope is that we
will cutover to this new technology sometime in
April/May of this year.
Steve
President’s Challenge:
•
February is - “Texture”
•
March - “Juxtapose” – two, or more pieces, that
complement each other.
•
April - “Natural Edge” (to allow a little extra
time to source your material.)
I’m very happy to report the return of Bruce’s popular Tech Talk recaps. Also, this month, we have an
article by Cathy Friesen documenting the creation
of the platter featured on this month’s cover.
Dex Hallwood has submitted a touching article
about his experience turning spinning tops for
young patients undergoing life changing surgeries
in Mombasa, Kenya.
This month, our Member Profile features long time
member Dan Lemire.
Thanks to everyone who contributed articles for
our newsletter this month. I’m looking forward to
hopefully receiving more articles for next month.
I’m sure you’ve all got a woodturning story, tip, or
interesting project just waiting to be told! Email
articles or questions to editor@gvwg.ca
Steve

Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 4
Advice was asked regarding a live centre not
holding properly in its Morse taper.
Marco suggested that it may be that there is something stuck in the back of female end of the Morse
taper. Marco suggested that a reamer had to be
used carefully as it actually removes metal from
the taper. Michael suggested using a plastic Morse
taper cleaner which reduces the risk of damaging
the alignment of the taper. Michael mentioned
that the cleaner, rather than the reamer, can be
purchased Amazon at a reasonable cost.
Dave suggested a cleaner can be made by using
sticky back sandpaper on the original Morris taper
itself.
Pippa said that when she was doing metal working
a common practice was to clean both the female
and the male taper during every use. A good practice to transport into our woodworking as well.
Donald wondered out loud if the problem could be
rust in the tailstock being that the lathe is quite a
bit older and there is a good chance that that may
also be part of the problem. That could be cleared
up with a reamer/cleaner as well.
Alan discovered that a small bit of CA glue had
dropped onto the outside of the Morse taper and
hardened into a noticeable lump. A few minutes
work with the diamond home was able to clean off
the glue and that solved the problem.
Brian went on to suggest that the club should probably buy a number two reamer to be kept in the
KMS shop and used to service the lathes so that
this problem does not happen in the shop.
Dealing with nasty hole left after drilling
Following on from Pippa’s pillbox demonstration,
Michael shared that he had two Forstner bits with
the points removed so that they didn’t leave that
nasty hole at the end of drilling. Some may recall
that that was a trick shown to us by Jack de Vos
some years ago who was doing the same thing with
spade bits to solve the same problem.
(Continued on page 5)
Tech Talk is held on the Monday evening following
the Guild ZOOM session. The credentials for the
session are sent to all registered Guild members
and all are encouraged to participate in the freeflowing discussion centered on technical aspects of
woodturning.

February 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 5
Drying Arbutus using a vacuum chamber
Gailine asked about vacuum drying as she has plans
to build a vacuum chamber from large diameter
steel pipe to dry an Arbutus log in the hopes of drying it without cracking. The general consensus was
that it may be very difficult as Arbutus is a very volatile wood. We suggested that it would be wiser to
plank the Arbutus and then dry it, but she was
quite adamant that she wanted to dry it whole.
I reported that I had tried using a vacuum chamber
to dry Maple with little success and also expressed
my opinion that vacuuming does not alter the very
natural character of the wood. However, being
quite adamant about drying the log in the whole
we asked her to keep us apprised on her success
Just the right tool for the job
Fraser told of a Detail Hand Scraper, sold by Lee
Valley, that proved to be perfect for removing
dried epoxy. There are three carbide heads; one
round, one triangular, the other square, so they
stay sharp for a long time. Should they dull, be
cautious trying sharpen on our CNB wheels. Carbide is very hard on the lungs and can lead to serious long term health issue.
Cleaning up hot glue
Pippa asked for advice on cleaning up hot glue on
green wood. Her problem was that the normal
methods of alcohol or paint thinner seem to leave
a gummy mess. We talked about several alternatives and also found a website that talked about
the various kinds of hot glue. Like CA glue, not all
not glues are created equal. Some melted at higher
temperatures than others. It was advised to get a
good quality high-temperature gun rather than the
crafters gun and to purchase higher quality white
glue sticks.
I then talked about the trick of using carpenters
glue and sizing your joint, allowing it to dry, and
then applying regular glue. A precise joint will set
very quickly and perhaps replace the need for hot
glue. This works primarily on end grain but the
technique can be used on cross grain as well.
Turning metals
Gailine asked about turning metal and we all
agreed that most non-ferrous metals such as copper, aluminum, brass and pewter can be turned
with standard high-speed turning tools. We also
discussed sanding metal afterwards and agreed
that, depending on the species, it may be best to
pre-finish the work before sanding metal to prevent smallish pieces of metal going into the grain of
the wood. This is certainly a problem with aluminum as it tends to leave a brown stain on light colored woods. I also used a burnishing compound
afterwards and that to can get into the grain of the
wood. Alternately some suggested simply sanding
to a very high grit, 600 or higher, and then not worrying about burnishing or finishing the metal.
Sanding speeds
Lucas is joined us for the first time and asked about
how fast to turn when sanding.
I suggested that heat is your enemy and if you’re
going to quickly or pressing too hard then sanding
can burn the wood or possibly induce heat checking. Another important factor is using good quality
sandpaper and that the FEPA standard paper
(those with a P in the front of the grit number) is
the best for woodturning and cloth backed is better
than paper backed. Also, not overusing the paper
once it plugged with dust. Either clean the paper
(Continued from page 4)
(Continued on page 6)
Detail Hand Scraper from Lee Valley

February 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 6
with a wire brush or crêpe or use of new piece of
paper. Long-held adage is “You should use sandpaper as though someone else was paying for it”.
We also talked about reverse sanding and, in the
case of spindle turning, while this lathe is stopped.
We then talked about over sanding in the case
where you hope to use a finishing product with either a stain or dye. Over sanding can cause the
grains to be plugged and for dyes and stains to be
absorbed unevenly.
Finally we expressed the importance of cleaning
the surface of your work between grits of sandpaper. Failure to do that will cause previous grits of
material to be caught on the finer sandpaper and
leave scratches which will appear when finish is
applied. It is enough to wipe with a clean cloth or
tack cloth or blow off with compressed air.
Recommended finish
Lucas then asked about finishes and we collectively
laughed because that is such a huge topic many
people immediately recommended Michael Dresdner’s book The New Wood Finishing Book as specific recommendations would depend on species,
final use of the product and environmental conditions.
One excellent suggestion was to look at the Instant
Gallery and ask the maker how they finished their
project, even going as far as to invite yourself to
their studio for a demonstration or hands-on practice.
Pippa also recommended buying a product that
you might find useful, trying it, and if you get the
result you want stick with that product. If it’s not
the kind of finish you want, go to the next product.
If you’re lucky you find one soon.
Sanding and finishing are one of the most important skills in woodturning. Most people gain
their experience through practice and sharing
openly with one another. Our advice to Lucas was
to ask questions of his peers. Invariably you will be
rewarded with a flood of information.
Grabbing bowl from the inside
Steve shared a creative modification to his scroll
chuck key to allow him to reach inside a deep bowl
in order to tighten or expand the jaws. This is often
hampered by the long handle on the chuck key
when reaching inside a deep bowl.
The handle was cut off and ground hex shaped. He
found that the correct sized socket wrench allows
him to reach inside bowl.
Angle grinder attachment for sanding
Marco showed recent purchase of an angle grinder
extension attachment that allows you to attach
sanding equipment for sanding the inside of deep
walls. It is available through Amazon and is quite
inexpensive. See details HERE.
(Continued from page 5)
Modified chuck key

Many years ago I was given a fir burl from a
friend’s barn. This friend also had a back yard
chicken coop and often gave me beautiful fresh
eggs.
At the American Woodturners Association Symposium in Portland in May 2024 Janice Levi demonstrated how to use egg shells as inlay. The light
went on and I knew exactly what I was going to
make for my friend.
We built a jig to hold it so my husband could chainsaw off a 3” slab.
I cut it round with a jigsaw then turned the platter.
The wood was very dry, hard and full of bark inclusions. Very challenging to turn. I had to sharpen
my gouges often.
After turning, I carved my maker’s mark on the
bottom. Then, using acrylic paint and the dry brush
technique, I completed my maker’s mark.
I applied Wipe-On Poly to the whole platter then
began the inlay.
The egg shells needed to have the membrane removed so I soaked them in warm water. Then using
my thumb and tweezers I peeled away the membrane attached to the inside of the shell.
I then tested some different coloured backgrounds
to decide which one would look best. I liked the
(Continued on page 8)

February 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 8
black.
Using Weld Bond and some water on a paint brush
I glued pieces of shell
to the recess I had
made in the rim. I
worked in small sections so that the glue
stayed soft and I could
move the shells slightly
for best fit. This stage
took about 5 full days to complete. It is very time
consuming.
The pitch had hardened to amber.
(Continued from page 7)

Bring your problems - Show off a new tool or invention - Share

Shopping at KMS Tools means you can help your
club earn credit - approximately 2% on your purchase. For instance, we recently used some of our
credit to buy the brand-new Laguna demo lathe
that we use for Focus on Fundamentals! All you
need to do is to link your name/phone number to
the GVWG and you’re done. The easiest way to do
this is to go online to: https://www.kmstools.com/
group-rewards and fill in a short form. In doing so,
you also become a KMS Club member and benefit
from better pricing on their full line of products. As
a friendly reminder if you are already a KMS Club
member, it is worthwhile to check that you are also
linked to the GVWG for us to receive the credits.

I was talking with my
new neighbour Jamie in
October last year. She
had moved in next door
from
England
while
working as a Paediatric
Anaesthesia Fellow at B
C Children’s Hospital.
During our conversation
she mentioned that she
had volunteered with
Operation Rainbow Canada, a 100% volunteer, non-profit medical services
organization that provides free reconstructive surgery and related health care for cleft lip and cleft
palate deformities to
needy children in developing countries. Their
latest mission was going to be held November 6-18 in Mombasa
Kenya. Jamie was chosen to be one of 28
doctors,
surgeons,
nurses
and
medical
support staff who had
volunteered their time
and expertise to fly to
Mombasa, Kenya to perform the surgeries. Without these repairs the children would face a multitude of medical issues during their life. Children
born with deformities are often shunned, ostracised, denied schooling and eventually succumb to
a solitary life lived in the protection of their homes.
Children fortunate enough to undergo surgery
spend a few days recovering in the hospital before returning home to
a better life. I was fascinated
by
the
programme and in awe of
the medical staff that
were volunteering their
time to bring a better
life to these children. I
thought of the frightening but life changing
surgeries that these
children
would
face
and wondered if there
was
anything
that
could be done to help
easy their anxiety before and after surgery. I
asked Jamie if I could
provide some colourful
spinning tops for her to give to the children facing
surgery. She thought that it was a good idea and
she offered to take them with her. I then got busy
turning tops and making sure that they were decorated with bright and lively colours. During the mission to Mombasa 19
complex reconstructive
surgeries
were
performed changing the
children’s lives forever.
When Jamie returned,
she shared a number of
photos that were taken
at Utange Field Hospital
in Mombasa. Permission to reproduce these
photographs was provided
by
Operation
Rainbow Canada. More
information on Operation Rainbow Canada including videos and a Global
News Report on the Mombasa mission can be
found on the Operation Rainbow Canada website:
https://www.operationrainbowcanada.ca/
missions/2024-mombasa-kenya
I am reaching out to ORC to see if there is interest
in our Guild providing spinning tops for future
medical missions.

February 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 10
“What’s a woodturner?”-a question that is often
asked in social gatherings or perhaps at a job interview when we proudly announce. “I am a
woodturner”. It is not possible to answer the question in a single sentence.
To describe woodturners, or just turners, is similar
to dealing with the philosophical concept of the
“universal” woodturner. We come in all sizes, colours, shapes and walks of life- from retired military
to students to world renowned scientists and politicians.
Turners are pre-teens to retired curmudgeons to
over-the-hill folks, many hills in fact. We all have
one thing in common. Whether or not it is a misplaced gene or a genetic modification we all love
wood, the solitude of wood, lathe and self.
Turning is the practice of” Wellness”. That new
health thing that we hear so much about. We are
mesmerized by transforming the natural wonder
that is wood into a work of art.
Turning is now, it is enjoying the moment and not
thinking about the problems past or the challenges
of the future. Turning is a form of meditation performed at different levels at different times in our
lives.
From novice to expert, this form of meditation
seems to be the unifying attraction - the taking of
oneself to another dimension and level of concentration. It is a cleansing of the mind of all else save
for our oneness with the wood riding the bevel.
We meld with the wood, we are fascinated by the
effect of the creation of an object from such a simple but complex material – wood. We are fascinated with the process from the first thought to the
end product or piece or work as woodturners like
to call it. It has many forms; from simple candle
sticks to complex segmented urns turned from
thousands of pieces stuck together with glue. Each
piece requires spinning on a lathe and sharp tools
motivated by a mind in the “now”.
Woodturners are designers, fabricators, technicians, dreamers, craftsmen, artists, creators. We
are scroungers in that whenever there is a piece of
wood lying helplessly on the ground we will stop
and look at it in hope we see a project; if we need a
tool, jig fixture we invent it and scrounge the material to make it from plastic, metal or what ever.
Most of all, turners are you and I common folk with
a passion to “just make stuff”. Mostly for ourselves!
We are not loners or recluses however, we love to
turn while someone watches, take break for a
coffee while we share information about the piece
on the lathe. We love to gather in small or large
groups and sip a wee dram to compare and share,
to discuss and pontificate, to brag and congratulate, to teach and be taught but best of all to share
joy of being a turner and the wellness of mind,
body and spirit it provides.
This is an article that originally appeared in a
GVWG newsletter many years ago and has been
updated by Merv and reprinted here.
Merv dedicates this article to Larry Stevenson.

Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 11
My maternal grandfather was a German master
carpenter and my Lemire ancestry can be traced
back to, two (2) brothers from France, both of
whom signed their names with the carpenter’s insignia when they landed at the port of Quebec City,
7 or 8 generation back.
I feel that I was inspired by my linage to create objects out of wood. I took all the Industrial Arts classes offered at High School in Smither BC and realized early on that I had a natural ability to use tools
and turn designs into tangible objects.
I opted for a career in Helicopter maintenance,
which provided good earnings, was challenging/
inspirational/rewarding and afforded me the opportunity to travel. This travel exposed me to a
wide variety of cultures and visual arts.
After many years of working and living out of a
suitcase, in 1979 I bought a house in Richmond.
My instructions to the real-estate agent was brief,
find me “A garage, with a house attached”.
I started building furniture using the school shops
on night school courses and finishing in my unheated garage. I bought tools as I needed them and
learned woodwork techniques from books and VHS
woodwork tapes. Also, Norm Abram was a must
watch on PBS.
An introduction by Rick Bellflower to the Pacific
Woodworkers Guild, PWWG broadened my woodworking scope and introduced me to a host of talented woodworkers in the lower mainland. Art
Leistman, Steve Fairbairn, Marco Berera, Steve
Hansen, John Hammond, all of whom are in the
GVWG. In addition, notables in the PWWG were
Bob Bedier, Bill Fox, Rob Prince, Peter Rainer, Klaas
Focker, Denis Reid, Fred Otte and Doug Morrison.
Doug Morrison, a master Ships Carver gave a short
“Relief Carving” course and that started me on a
new course of more hands on artistic and creative
woodwork.
I followed up Doug’s introduction with a week long
work shop in Portland Oregon at the University of
the Roses. Nora Hall a professional carver in her
80’s took us through the techniques of European
relief carving. Grape clusters, tree leaves, swirls,
(Continued on page 12)

February 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 12
corbels, lettering, etc. She taught the technique of
using a V gouge to trace out the pattern, then U
gouges to relief down the wood to create a 3D
effect.
My introduction to woodturning came when fellow
member in the PWWG, Klass Focker decided to sell
his Delta Lathe. I bought Klaas’s Lathe and I bought
from Ian Waymark, who at the time was importing
Technatool (now Nova) Lathes and tools from New
Zealand, a big honking turning
gouge that had a replaceable
tip. I found some blocks of
green wood by the side of the
road and turned out about 30
bowl blanks. Lots of catches,
spooked myself many times,
but managed to figure out how
to hog out a bowl blank. That
was 30 years ago and I’m still
using some of those bowl
blanks.
I have moved from my original house in Richmond
and we now have a house in Steveston. I once
again got my garage, but this time it was fully detached. The 2 car garage has never seen a car in it
and it is my work shop. It is equipped with all the
standard stationary equipment, table saw, band
saw, radial arm saw, drill press, planer and disc
sander. Space is a limited due to the large inventory of wood that I have collected and keep in my
shop.
I have upgraded to a Nova DVR 3000, variable
speed Lathe and I have a wide array of gouges,
skews and scrapers, some home made.
For turning, I prefer local woods such as maple,
birch, walnut, cherry, yellow cedar, black locus,
London plane, etc.. My favourite wood to turn is
Holly, but it’s hard to find big pieces that are not
spilt and cracked. My pride and joy Holly turning,
is a bowl that I call “Pure Simplicity”.
I like to buff the wood where ever possible and I
use, a variety of finishing products depending on
the application or use of the object. Wipe on Poly,
Carnauba wax, spray lacquer, shellac, tung oil, water based varathane all work well for finishing.
I’ve thought about incorporation other materials
into my turnings, but to date I have not been brave
enough to try! Having said that , I used alkaline
stains and acrylic paint to liven up some projects.
(Continued from page 11)
(Continued on page 13)

February 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 13
I do more wood carving, than wood turning and
would like to incorporate more of my carving into
my turnings. So far, I’ve turned a dome shape then
did a relief carving of a Green Man and I turned
plate in order to try out a Celtic Knot design that I
learned in one of the GVWG weekend demos.
I get ideas from various sources. The GVWG is one
of the best places I get inspiration and ideas. I
used to buy and read turning magazines, but don’t
do that much anymore. There is plenty of YouTube
videos that provide ideas, instruction and inspiration for unique new projects.
I’m not sure I can say who or what has had the
greatest influence on what I create out of wood.
I’m a bit like a sponge, soaking up ideas that I find
interesting to try and turn into physical objects. I
suppose I’m pretty much a realist and I lean towards functionality verses pure artistic purpose in
what I create.
Hollow turning is by far the hardest challenge for
me. I have done a number of hollowed out vessels,
but have never been comfortable with the turning
process, it scares me! My Genie hollowed vessel
was made in two pieces and glued together. It
took me many months to complete, however I did
(Continued from page 12)
(Continued on page 14)

February 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 14
learn a lot in the process.
My favourite project has to be the disc which I
turned out of Walnut to reveal a unique wood
grain pattern, forming the shape of a fish head. I’m
fascinated by this one-time event, that will never
to be repeated, exposing the image that was
trapped in the wood. Without my aid by putting
sharp tool to spinning wood, the image would have
stayed hidden and would never been admired and
appreciated.
I’m open to letting my work go in any direction that
suites my ability and fascination. I expect my skills
to improve in some areas and to diminish in other
aspects. It is all in tune with the creative process.
I will try new techniques that I think are within my
level of skill and development. There is no particular technique that I’m desperate to try. Although I
would like to take on a fairy complicated project
with carving incorporated into the woodturning.
I don’t sell my work commercially; however, I do
take on small commissions from friends. I like
making something for someone that I think will appreciate it and for the most part can’t get it anywhere else.
I’m not afraid to show my work and I’m mostly
looking to get constructive feedback and/or its nice
to get accolades.
I display my work at the Richmond Carving show
and in the Gallery at the GVWG meetings.
(Continued from page 13)

 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock

with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage and GVWG Safety
webpage.
